claims.text: Boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum plating can have microstructures that permit molten aluminum infiltration.
Controlled atmospheric plasma oxidation at approximately 700°C will produce an ultra-thin oxide barrier on boride-based components.
The plasma-produced barrier will be dense and adherent.
The plasma-produced barrier may consist of an oxide or mixed oxide-boride phase.
The plasma-produced oxide layer will be self-healing.
Atmospheric plasma treatment promotes rapid surface oxidation.
The compact oxide layer will limit aluminum diffusion into the component.
The compact oxide layer will limit chemical attack by molten aluminum.
Plasma-oxidized boride-based components will have a lower corrosion rate than untreated components under otherwise identical molten-aluminum exposure.
Plasma-oxidized boride-based components will exhibit less aluminum infiltration than untreated components.
The improvement is expected to remain effective during molten-aluminum exposure at 660–700°C under standard hot-dip plating conditions.
Mechanical abrasion of the oxide layer may compromise the corrosion-resistance improvement.
Treatment parameters outside an optimized range may compromise the corrosion-resistance improvement.
The exact plasma-oxidation temperature and duration needed to produce an effective barrier are uncertain.
The long-term stability of the barrier under cyclic thermal conditions is uncertain.
